processing: Sun-dried sheng maocha from a small stand of old trees, kept loose or pressed, with no ripe-style fermentation.
harvest_season: Spring old-tree leaf is what the name trades on; the fresh leaf is hard to pick and scarce.
appearance_dry: Dark green, thick rope-like strands with long stems.
taste_profile: Sweet, smooth and thick-bodied with very little bitterness or astringency, and a faint cooling mint-like feeling behind a lingering fragrance.

brewing.notes: A soft Yiwu-style tea that takes full heat well. Do not cut steeps too short or it will seem thin.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, like other sheng, in very small lots of spring old-tree tea. Its price jumped sharply in a short time, so counterfeits are a real risk. Picking in state forests has been under enforcement, and at least one spring price index left out Bohetang for that reason, so ask how recent lots were sourced.
description:
Bohetang is a tiny place deep in the Yiwu tea area of Mengla County, at about 1,800 metres, reached by a rough mountain road. The name means mint pond; one account ties it to wild mint growing there, another to a pond beside a few old trees.

What made it famous is scarcity. One count puts the large trees at 33, the rest of the old trees being much smaller, and output of sun-dried tea at no more than 200 kilograms.

In the cup it is described as restrained Yiwu at its most extreme: soft and sweet, thick, nearly free of bitterness, with a faint cool mint feeling. Most of this description comes from people selling or championing it, so taste before you trust.

The homophone spelling 薄荷糖, mint candy, is common and refers to the same tea. With so few trees and such high prices, a lot of what carries this name deserves suspicion. Ask for the year, the maker and the size of the lot.
history:
Accounts say tea here was once worth so little that many large trees were cut for building shelters, leaving the few that survive. Its price then climbed from several hundred yuan per kilogram to 8,000 within two years, putting it among the leaders in Yiwu; the year is not recorded.

The location is described in slightly different ways, with one account placing it under Manla village committee within the old Mansa tea mountain. Later, Xishuangbanna authorities acted against picking and planting tea in state forest, and Bohetang was named among the state-forest mountains left off a spring price index.
